D. Judicial Precedents and Agile Workflow Audit Risks

Recent federal appellate and Tax Court decisions demonstrate that even when a software project is properly categorized under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6), the IRS and the courts will disallow 100% of the claimed credit if the taxpayer cannot substantiate outset technical uncertainty under IRC § 174 and the 80% process-of-experimentation fraction under IRC § 41(d)(1)(C) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(6) at the granular business-component level.

In Little Sandy Coal Company, Inc. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2021-15 (Docket No. 17431-17, decided February 11, 2021), aff'd, 62 F.4th 287 (7th Cir. March 7, 2023), both the U.S. Tax Court and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit upheld the IRS's complete disallowance of research tax credits claimed by a shipbuilding subsidiary (Corn Island Shipyard) for the design and construction of a first-in-class tanker barge and a floating drydock. The case established three critical legal principles directly applicable to Dual Function Software audits:

items: Strict Enforcement of the 80% Process-of-Experimentation Fraction: Under IRC § 41(d)(1)(C) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(6), the taxpayer must demonstrate that at least 80% of the research activities with respect to the business component—measured on a cost or other consistently applied reasonable basis—constituted elements of a process of experimentation. As the Seventh Circuit noted at 62 F.4th 287, 298, qualified research under Section 41 cannot merely be "any design or modification to meet customer specifications," nor routine testing to confirm a product design is appropriate, but must remove technical uncertainty related to the development or improvement of the component.

Inclusion of Direct Support and Supervision in the Numerator—Only If Substantiated: On appeal, the Seventh Circuit disagreed with the Tax Court's apparent categorical exclusion of production, direct support, and direct supervision activities (IRC § 41(b)(2)(B)(ii) and 26 CFR § 1.41-2(c)) from the numerator of the 80% "substantially all" fraction, holding that direct support and supervisory personnel can be included in the numerator if their activities directly support or constitute elements of a process of experimentation. Nevertheless, the Seventh Circuit affirmed the disallowance because the taxpayer relied on retrospective oral testimony and arbitrary trial estimates rather than contemporaneous documentation quantifying experimental versus non-experimental activities—famously observing that "Section 41(d) requires us to walk by sight, not by faith".

Inability to Invoke the Shrinking-Back Rule Without Subcomponent Accounting: Under the shrinking-back rule of 26 CFR § 1.41-4(b)(2), if an overall business component fails the Four-Part Test (for example, because less than 80% of activities on the overall system were experimental), the tests are applied to the most significant subset of elements of the product or software until a qualifying subcomponent is reached. In Little Sandy Coal, because the taxpayer adopted an "all-or-nothing" strategy claiming the entire vessel and failed to maintain subcomponent-level time and cost accounting, neither the taxpayer nor the court could apply the shrinking-back rule to salvage credits for novel subcomponents.

body.text: In Phoenix Design Group, Inc. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2024-113 (Docket No. 4759-22, Judge Greaves, decided December 23, 2024), the U.S. Tax Court disallowed all claimed research credits across three sampled mechanical, electrical, plumbing, and fire protection (MEPF) engineering projects for research years 2013 through 2016 (credit carryforward years 2015 through 2019) and sustained accuracy-related penalties. The Tax Court's holdings in Phoenix Design Group reinforce four major audit pitfalls for software and engineering taxpayers:

items: Objective Outset Uncertainty Under IRC § 174 vs. Ongoing Design Revisions: Citing 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(5), Max v. Commissioner (T.C. Memo. 2021-37), and Betz v. Commissioner (T.C. Memo. 2023-84), the Tax Court held that technical uncertainty is an objective standard based on the information available to the taxpayer at the outset of research. The court rejected Phoenix Design Group's (PDG's) argument that objective uncertainty persisted across the entire MEPF system throughout construction merely because engineers had to alter or revise designs in later stages; if gross-block diagrams and schematic design documents already establish the basic design of the system, localized revisions do not render the entire system uncertain.

Subcomponent Uncertainty Does Not Contaminate the Whole System: The court held that technical uncertainty regarding a single subset or subcomponent of a business component does not establish that the design of the entire business component is uncertain as a whole, rejecting sparse, conclusory engineer testimony that a change in one subcomponent impacted the basic design of the entire system.

Rejection of Theoretical Iterative Frameworks Conflicting with Employee Timesheets: PDG argued that its formal six-stage design process inherently mirrored the scientific method required under Union Carbide Corp. and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(5)(i) whenever engineers reverted to earlier stages. The Tax Court rejected this high-level framework argument because it focuses on the actual, granular activities of employees, and pointed out glaring inconsistencies in PDG's employee hour sheets: employees never categorized tracked hours by design phase, and narrative descriptions directly contradicted PDG's theoretical framework—for example, on the VU ESB Project, mechanical engineer Ross T. Malloy logged hours during the "design development" stage as "finishing up construction documents" (which PDG defined as the final stage), while on the BHNM Oxford Project, mechanical engineer John Wade logged hours during the "design development" stage as "schematic design" (an earlier, separate stage).

Failure of Subcomponents Even After Applying the Shrinking-Back Rule: Unlike Little Sandy Coal, the Tax Court in Phoenix Design Group explicitly applied the shrinking-back rule of 26 CFR § 1.41-4(b)(2) to evaluate the next most significant subcomponents—the individual mechanical, electrical, and plumbing systems (including PDG's claim of uncertainty regarding the hospital location and sizing of an HVAC system)—and held that even at the shrunk-back subcomponent level, PDG failed to demonstrate that ≥80% of employee activities constituted a scientific-method process of experimentation.

body.text: These judicial holdings create acute Risk Amplification in Agile Software Environments. Modern enterprise software engineering relies on cross-functional agile scrum teams working in rapid two-week sprints where a single developer's sprint backlog routinely blends qualified experimental algorithm development with non-qualified backlog grooming, UI styling, routine bug patches, data migration, and G&A workflow configuration. Under Little Sandy Coal and Phoenix Design Group, if an enterprise developing Dual Function Software merely exports aggregate sprint hours or generic ticket labels (e.g., "Sprint 14 development," "ERP integration," or "bug fixes") without mapping developer hours to (1) segregated functional subsets (TSS vs. Dual-Function Subset vs. G&A Core) as required for Form 6765 Section G and (2) specific technical uncertainties and iterative hypothesis testing, the IRS can disallow both the Dual Function Software segmentation and the underlying Section 41(d) qualification.

body.text: VII. Strategic Recommendations and Compliance Next Steps
A. Refining Guidance on the 10% Usage Threshold: From General Examples to Industry Safe-Harbor Protocols

While 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(vi)(C) and Section V of the Preamble to T.D. 9786 already establish an "objective, reasonable method within the taxpayer's industry" standard and enumerate four concrete measurement methods—processing time, amount of data transfer, number of software user interface screens, and number of third-party initiated functions—substantive audit controversies still arise over how taxpayers weight and project those metrics in modern cloud-native and microservice architectures.

For example, in an enterprise platform where an internal G&A financial batch-reconciliation job runs nightly for four continuous hours while external customers execute hundreds of thousands of sub-second REST or GraphQL API calls throughout the business day, measuring "use" by raw server processing time versus number of third-party initiated functions or amount of data transfer can produce substantially different usage percentages. Similarly, headless API-driven microservices and backend event-streaming engines have no traditional "software user interface screens". While Treasury regulations deliberately grant flexibility by permitting any objective, reasonable method within the taxpayer's industry, administrative updates to the IRS Research Credit Audit Techniques Guide (ATG) or a dedicated Revenue Procedure establishing standardized pre-development forecasting protocols for cloud, API, and event-driven architectures would substantially reduce examination disputes without requiring an amendment to 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(vi)(C).
B. Administrative Closure Under the 25% Safe Harbor vs. Maximizing the Third-Party Subset

Because 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(vi)(A)–(C) and the IRS Instructions for Form 6765 already structure the 25% safe harbor as a mutually exclusive elective alternative to the three-part HTIT for a given Dual-Function Subset—meaning that electing the 25% safe harbor caps includible QREs of that subset at 25% and forfeits the remaining 75% without an HTIT examination—taxpayers do not need a regulatory amendment to avoid litigating the HTIT on the 75% residual of a safe-harbor subset.

Instead, the primary strategic imperative for enterprise taxpayers is minimizing the size of the interwoven Dual-Function Subset before the 25% safe harbor is applied. Every engineering hour and cloud-computing dollar that is architecturally decoupled from the shared G&A core and isolated into a pure Third-Party Subset (TSS) under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(vi)(B) achieves a 100% QRE inclusion rate rather than a 25% QRE inclusion rate—quadrupling the eligible research credit base for those expenditures while leaving only the inseparable shared algorithmic core subject to the 75% safe-harbor haircut.
C. Taxpayer Best Practices: Integrated Project-Inception Compliance Protocol

To withstand heightened IRS examination scrutiny under Little Sandy Coal (62 F.4th 287), Phoenix Design Group (T.C. Memo. 2024-113), IRS Field Attorney Advice 20212501F, and mandatory Form 6765 Section G business-component reporting (effective for tax years beginning after 2025), taxpayers developing Dual Function Software should institutionalize a five-step contemporaneous compliance protocol at the beginning of every software development project:

items: Charter-Stage Intent and Architectural Subset Mapping (26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(v) & (vi)(D)): Prior to writing machine-readable code, conduct a joint engineering-and-tax architecture review that formally documents the software's intended internal G&A and external third-party capabilities at the outset of development, and partitions the system into discrete business components: (a) pure Internal Use Software / G&A modules under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(iii) (Form 6765 Category A), (b) pure Third-Party Subsets under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(vi)(B) (Category B — TSS), and (c) interwoven Dual-Function Subsets under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(vi)(C) (Category B — Safe Harbor).

Third-Party Boundary Verification and Vendor Exclusion Audit (26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(vi)(E) & Example 6): Audit every external-facing portal, EDI feed, and API endpoint to verify that the external users qualify as "third parties" (such as external customers initiating orders, transfers, or data queries) and strip out any interfaces used by vendors, suppliers, or contractors to support the taxpayer's own G&A functions (such as vendor inventory replenishment under Example 6 or accounts payable invoicing portals), which must be classified as pure IUS.

Contemporaneous ≥10% Third-Party Usage Forecast (26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(vi)(C)–(D)): For each interwoven Dual-Function Subset (evaluated separately after excluding any isolated TSS, as required by Example 14), preserve a dated, pre-development engineering estimate demonstrating that third-party usage is reasonably anticipated at the beginning of development to constitute at least 10% of the subset's total use, utilizing one or more of the four regulatory metrics: processing time, amount of data transfer, number of software user interface screens, or number of third-party initiated functions.

Subcomponent-Level Agile Time Tracking and ERP Cost Segregation (26 CFR § 1.41-2(d), § 1.41-4(d), PLR 200236028, & CCA 201549024): Configure agile project-management repositories (e.g., Jira epics, component tags, and payroll timecodes) so that developer, direct supervisor, and direct support hours map directly to the discrete software subsets required for Form 6765 Section G (Columns 49(c)–(e) and 50–56). Simultaneously, segregate non-qualifying ERP option selection and embedded template implementation costs (which must be capitalized under IRC § 263(a) and amortized over 36 months under IRC § 167(f)(1) per PLR 200236028 and CCA 201549024) from custom machine-readable code development.

Outset Technical Uncertainty and Scientific-Method Experimentation Logs (IRC § 41(d)(1), Little Sandy Coal, & Phoenix Design Group): For each qualifying Third-Party Subset and Dual-Function Subset, require lead engineers to record at the start of development the specific objective technological uncertainties (IRC § 174 and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(3)) regarding capability, method, or appropriate design, the alternative architectures or algorithms evaluated, and the modeling, simulation, or systematic trial-and-error testing conducted—ensuring that time-tracking narratives align with experimental phases and substantiate that ≥80% of the subset's research activities constituted elements of a process of experimentation for a qualified purpose under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(5)–(6).

cells: Statutory Enactment Lineage and Incremental Credit Structure under IRC § 41(a)
26 U.S.C. § 41(a); ERTA 1981 § 221 (Pub. L. 97-34); H.R. Rep. No. 97-201; IRS ATG (updated July 2, 2026); IRS PLR 201006027

Confirmed 1981 enactment to stimulate capital formation, productivity, and private R&D spending, and the incremental structure (20% of QREs over base amount plus 20% of basic research and energy consortium payments under 26 U.S.C. § 41(a)(1)–(3)). Refined statutory lineage: originally enacted in 1981 as IRC § 44F, redesignated as IRC § 30 in 1984, redesignated as IRC § 41 in 1986, and made permanent by the PATH Act of 2015.
Upfront Timing of Determination Based on Taxpayer Intent at Project Inception

Confirmed verbatim under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(vi)(D): "A taxpayer must apply this paragraph (c)(6)(vi) based on the intent of the taxpayer and the facts and circumstances at the beginning of the software development" (effective for taxable years beginning on or after October 4, 2016).
Definition of Dual Function Software and Foundational Presumption of Internal Use
26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(vi)(A); T.D. 9786; IRS Instructions for Form 6765 (Rev. Jan. 2025 / Dec. 2025)

Confirmed under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(vi)(A): software developed both for internal G&A functions and to enable third-party interaction or allow third parties to initiate functions or review data is presumed to be developed primarily for internal use unless paragraph (c)(6)(vi)(B) (Third-Party Subset) or (c)(6)(vi)(C) (25% Safe Harbor) applies.
Exhaustive Definition of G&A Functions and Regulatory Citations for IUS vs. Non-IUS
26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(iii)(A)–(B) & (iv)(A)–(B); IRS Instructions for Form 6765

Verified the three exhaustive G&A categories: Financial Management, Human Resources Management, and Support Services. Corrected regulatory citations: Internal Use Software and the three G&A categories are codified in 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(iii) ((iii)(A) and (iii)(B)(1)–(3), Form 6765 Category A), whereas 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(iv)(A) governs commercial software held for sale, lease, license, or marketing (Form 6765 Category C Non-IUS).
Isolation of the Third-Party Subset (TSS) and 100% QRE Eligibility

Confirmed under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(vi)(B) and Examples 11 and 14: a segregated subset of elements that only enables third-party interaction or allows third parties to initiate functions or review data overcomes the internal-use presumption, is treated as Non-IUS under (c)(6)(iv)(B), and qualifies 100% of its allocable QREs under the standard Four-Part Test.
Exclusion of G&A Support Vendors from the Regulatory Definition of "Third Party"
26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(vi)(E) & (viii) Example 6; T.D. 9786

Corrected: Under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(vi)(E), "third parties do not include any persons that use the software to support the general and administrative functions of the taxpayer." In Example 6, software enabling electronic interaction and function initiation with vendors for inventory management is held to be pure Internal Use Software (not third-party interaction or Dual Function Software) because inventory management is a G&A financial management function under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(iii)(B)(1).
Standard Four-Part Test Permitted Purpose vs. HTIT Cost Reduction Standard

Verified the Four-Part Test and the 80% process-of-experimentation rule (26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(6)). Corrected Permitted Purpose: under IRC § 41(d)(3)(A) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(5)(ii), a qualified purpose under the Four-Part Test is limited to new or improved function, performance, reliability, or quality. Substantial and economically significant "reduction in cost" is the standard for the Innovative prong of the HTIT under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(vii)(B).
Non-Qualifying ERP Configuration vs. IRC § 263(a) Capitalization of Embedded Templates

Confirmed non-qualified ERP configuration and routine data mapping under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(8). Confirmed under PLR 200236028 and CCA 201549024 that technical consulting costs for option selection and implementing embedded ERP templates (plus allocable modeling/design costs and undefined miscellaneous costs) do not constitute writing machine-readable code under Rev. Proc. 2000-50 and must be capitalized under IRC § 263(a) and 26 CFR § 1.263(a)-4(c)(1)(xiv) & (g)(1) and amortized ratably over 36 months under IRC § 167(f)(1).
Distinction Between Software Excepted from the HTIT ((c)(6)(ii)) and Non-IUS ((c)(6)(iv))
26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(ii)(A)–(C) & (iv)(A)–(B); IRS Instructions for Form 6765

Corrected regulatory classification: 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(ii) (Inapplicability of the HTIT, Form 6765 Category D) covers only the three internal-use exceptions: (ii)(A) used in qualified research, (ii)(B) used in a qualified production process, and (ii)(C) integral hardware-software package (Example 1). Commercial/SaaS software sold, leased, licensed, or marketed to third parties is governed by 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(iv)(A) (Form 6765 Category C Non-IUS).
Three-Part High Threshold of Innovation Test (HTIT) and Rejection of the "Unique or Novel" Standard
26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(vii)(A)–(D); T.D. 9786 Preamble Sec. VII

Verified all three HTIT prongs and the exact language in 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(vii)(C) that "substantial uncertainty" requires a higher level of uncertainty and technical risk than non-IUS components. Corrected the Innovation prong description: 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(vii)(B) explicitly rejects any requirement that software be unique, novel, or significantly different from existing implementation methods ("not a determination of the unique or novel nature of the software").
25% Safe Harbor Mechanics and ≥10% Anticipated Third-Party Usage Requirement

Confirmed under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(vi)(C) and (D): 25% QRE inclusion applies if the underlying research activities satisfy IRC § 41(d) (without regard to § 41(d)(4)(E)) and third-party use is reasonably anticipated at the beginning of software development to constitute at least 10% of the Dual Function Software's or Dual-Function Subset's total use.
Enumerated Objective Industry Methods for Measuring the 10% Usage Threshold
26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(vi)(C) & (viii) Example 14; T.D. 9786 Preamble Sec. V

Corrected: 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(vi)(C) forbids subjective standards by mandating an "objective, reasonable method within the taxpayer's industry" and expressly enumerating acceptable methods in the regulatory text: processing time, amount of data transfer, and number of software user interface screens (plus number of third-party initiated functions in Section V of the T.D. 9786 Preamble).
Availability of the 25% Safe Harbor When No Separate Third-Party Subset Can Be Identified
26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(vi)(C) & (viii) Example 12; T.D. 9786 Preamble Sec. V

Corrected: Directly established by 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(vi)(C) ("there remains dual function software or a subset..."), Section V of the T.D. 9786 Preamble ("serves as a benefit for taxpayers who cannot identify a separate third-party subset"), and Example 12, where Taxpayer X "is unable to identify a third party subset" and is explicitly permitted to include 25% ($12,500 of $50,000) of the entire Dual Function Software's QREs under the safe harbor because anticipated third-party use is 15% (≥10%).
Codification of Research Credit Recordkeeping and Substantiation Mandate

Verified the verbatim recordkeeping quotation and required financial/technical records, and clarified the exact legal authority: the requirement to "retain records in sufficiently usable form and detail to substantiate that the expenditures claimed are eligible for the credit" is codified in 26 CFR § 1.41-4(d) (cross-referencing 26 CFR § 1.6001-1 and IRC § 6001), rather than in the statutory text of IRC § 41.
Coordination of the Employee Wage 80% Rule (26 CFR § 1.41-2(d)(2)) and Business-Component 80% Rule (26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(6))

Confirmed that under IRC § 41(b)(2)(B) and 26 CFR § 1.41-2(d)(2), 100% of an employee's annual wages qualify if ≥80% of the employee's services are qualified services, while under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(6) the 80% process-of-experimentation rule applies separately to each business component without regard to § 1.41-2(d)(2), and employee wages must still be allocated across the 100%-eligible TSS and 25%-eligible Dual-Function Subset.
Judicial Holdings in Little Sandy Coal (2021/2023) and Phoenix Design Group (2024)
Little Sandy Coal Co., Inc. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2021-15, aff'd, 62 F.4th 287 (7th Cir. 2023); Phoenix Design Group, Inc. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2024-113 (Dec. 23, 2024)

Confirmed both decisions and expanded with exact appellate and Tax Court holdings: Seventh Circuit's clarification on direct support/supervision in the 80% fraction numerator paired with affirmance for lack of contemporaneous time records in Little Sandy Coal (62 F.4th 287), and the Tax Court's rejection of ongoing construction revision uncertainty, citation of conflicting timesheet narratives (Malloy and Wade), and application of the shrinking-back rule (26 CFR § 1.41-4(b)(2)) to individual MEPF subcomponents in Phoenix Design Group (T.C. Memo. 2024-113).
Mandatory Business Component and Software Category Disclosure on IRS Form 6765 Section G
IRS Instructions for Form 6765 (Rev. Jan. 2025 / updated Dec. 2025); IR-2021-203 & June 18, 2024 Update

Confirmed Section G effective dates (optional before 2026 unless amended; mandatory after 2025 subject to QSB and ≤$1.5M QRE/≤$50M gross receipts exceptions), the 80%/Top 50 descending-order reporting rule, Column 49(d) (3. All Others), and Column 49(e) software codes: A (IUS), B (DFS), C (Non-IUS), and D (Excepted from IUS treatment).
Elective Finality of the 25% Safe Harbor vs. HTIT Audit on the Disallowed 75% Residual
26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(vi)(A)–(C) & (viii) Examples 12–14; T.D. 9786 Preamble; IRS Form 6765 Instructions

Corrected: Under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(vi)(A)–(C) and Examples 12 and 14, the 25% safe harbor is already an elective alternative to the HTIT for a Dual-Function Subset. Electing the 25% safe harbor fixes includible QREs of that subset at 25% and excludes the remaining 75% without subjecting that 75% residual to an HTIT examination.
